title: Every RCM Vendor Says "AI-Powered." Here's How CFOs Can Tell Who Can Prove It.
summary: Five common mistakes in AI revenue cycle vendor evaluations, plus a free RFP template and scoring workbook for healthcare finance leaders.
body_markdown:
Ask five revenue cycle vendors whether their platform uses AI, and you'll get five yeses. Ask them to show which recovered dollars trace back to which claims, and the field narrows quickly.


That gap matters more than ever. In the AMA's December 2025 survey of 1,000 physicians, physicians reported completing an average of 40 prior authorizations a week, consuming about 13 hours of physician and staff time ([AMA](https://www.ama-assn.org/system/files/prior-authorization-survey.pdf) ). Payer rules are changing on a timeline measured in months: under CMS's prior authorization rule (CMS-0057-F), Medicare Advantage, Medicaid, and CHIP plans have had to meet new decision deadlines since January 2026, with electronic prior authorization APIs required by January 2027 ([CMS](https://www.cms.gov/newsroom/fact-sheets/cms-interoperability-and-prior-authorization-final-rule-cms-0057-f) ).


Finance leaders are under real pressure to automate, and the vendor market is crowded with similar-sounding promises. In our experience, the hardest part isn't finding vendors. It's running an evaluation that separates the ones who can prove results from the ones who can only describe them. Most RFP templates were built for an earlier generation of software, and they reward the wrong things.


## Five ways AI revenue cycle evaluations go wrong


### 1. Letting the vendor size the opportunity


When a vendor's projection is the only number in the room, you're negotiating on their terms. Before the first demo, pull your own baseline using standard definitions, such as HFMA's MAP Keys for denial write-offs, net days in A/R, and cost to collect, and build your own estimate. Keep run-rate benefits separate from one-time backlog recovery. Cleaning up aged A/R can make year one look spectacular, but only the run-rate pays for a multi-year contract.


### 2. Treating roadmap answers like live capabilities


In a written RFP response, "yes" can mean live in production, available after configuration, possible with custom development, or dependent on a third party. Those are very different commitments. Require vendors to label every answer with its status, and score accordingly.


### 3. Choosing based on the demo


Demos run on curated data. The only reliable test is a short pilot that gives every finalist the same data set and the same success metrics, agreed in writing before it starts. For coding, include charts your team has already audited, so accuracy claims can be checked against your own coders. Ask each vendor to run one routine case and one difficult case, with missing or conflicting documentation, from start to finish.


### 4. Screening out vendors on size


Many RFPs set minimums for years in business or annual revenue. Those thresholds measure size, not results, and can eliminate capable vendors before you see what they can do. Screen instead on what matters to your operation: live production use in your specialty, integration with your EHR, current security attestations, and willingness to pilot on your data. Make those pass/fail gates, so a strong overall score can't hide a missing must-have.


### 5. Ignoring how the vendor gets paid


Pricing models shape vendor behavior. Contingency pricing can mean paying a percentage on dollars you would have collected anyway. Per-unit pricing is predictable, but ask whether failed attempts and retries are billed. Subscriptions are easy to budget but can leave you paying for capacity you don't use. Whatever the model, negotiate performance guarantees, a written method for attributing recovered dollars, and clear exit terms before you sign.


## Four questions that separate strong vendors


Good RFP questions are written so vague answers stand out. Here is one from each of the four areas where revenue most often leaks.


**Payer fee benchmarking:** *"Can you compare our contracted rates to what payers actually paid, and flag underpayments by code and payer?"* Published payer rate data is useful for negotiation, but it doesn't show you what you're owed today. Strong vendors connect benchmarks to your own remittances and quantify the shortfall in dollars.


**Prior authorization:** *"If a payer said no authorization was needed and later denies the claim, how does your platform respond?"* Look for a timestamped record of the original check and an appeal that uses it. That record is often what wins.


**Coding:** *"How do you report undercoding and overcoding?"* The answer should be both, reported separately, with dollar impact and compliance risk for each. A vendor that only finds missed revenue should worry your compliance team.


**Denials:** *"Which denials do you work, and how do you make sure none are missed?"* Denials that sit in EHR hold queues or aging buckets are often written off without anyone deciding to write them off. Strong vendors work all of them, including aged A/R.


## Get the full guide and scoring workbook


We put these lessons into a free, vendor-neutral resource for finance and revenue cycle leaders. It doesn't recommend any vendor, including us. It's designed to help you run a fair evaluation and hold every vendor to the same standard.


**The CFO's Guide to Evaluating AI Revenue Integrity Platforms** includes:


- **A business case framework** with baseline metrics built on HFMA definitions and a calculator for payback and three-year return.
- **What good looks like** in payer fee benchmarking, prior authorization, coding, and denials, plus the red flags to watch for.
- **59 RFP questions** , with 16 essentials tagged for a shorter first-round RFI and guidance on what a strong answer includes.
- **A ready-to-use scoring workbook** with weighted scoring, pass/fail gates, a scope brief to send vendors, a pilot tracker, and a decision log.
- **A comparison of pricing models** and the contract protections worth negotiating.
